lines: I.  Introduction

A scalar query measures q coordinates and must distinguish the truth from an alternative. The corpus states its per-sample information against an alternative parameterised by (d, x): d coordinates displaced by μ, the remaining q − d displaced by x.

Two objections stand against using that statement. First, a bound proved only over a two-parameter SLICE says nothing about alternatives outside it, so a lower bound quantified over (d, x) is not a lower bound over the class. Second, the design weights that reproduce the corpus's coefficients were FITTED — a consistent non-negative solution in 24 of 24 parameter cells is evidence that the coefficients come from the model, but it is not a derivation.
This work removes both objections. Neither is answered by more cells or more search; each needs an argument.
II.  Contributions

C1.  THE SLICE IS NOT A RESTRICTION. We define the general alternative as an arbitrary shift vector, show the (d, x) formula is exactly that general information evaluated on the slice, and prove that EVERY alternative in the class costs at least the slice value. A lower bound quantified over the slice is therefore a lower bound over the whole class, and the two-parameter family stops being a limitation.
C2.  THE SLICE IS EXACTLY TIGHT. The bound of C1 is attained precisely on the slice, so it cannot be improved by enlarging the class — the reduction loses nothing and gains nothing.

C3.  NO BLIND DIRECTION AT ALL. The general information vanishes only at the zero shift, so the scalar query is blind in no direction whatsoever. This restates the asymmetry against the pair query without reference to the slice.

C4.  THE DESIGN IS DERIVED, NOT FITTED. Reading the weights across all 24 cells shows they depend on the budget split η and the price c ALONE, and not on the model parameters (q, μ). We prove the two weights spend the unit budget exactly and that the budget constraint together with the split FORCES them, so nothing is left to fit.

C5.  WHERE A TRANSITION CAN OCCUR, DERIVED. Because the delivered information is affine in the split, the optimum sits at an endpoint unless the two queries buy information at exactly the same rate per unit price. We prove that condition, and that on it every split is optimal.
III.  Methodology
STEP 1 — THE GENERAL ALTERNATIVE  (C1).   Igen, IB_eq_of_slice

HOW IT IS CLOSED. The slice identity is a finite-sum computation: split the index set into S and its complement, evaluate the constant summand on each, and use the cardinality identity for the complement. The two expressions are then the same rational function, so the (d, x) formula and the general one are not two different models.
STEP 2 — THE REDUCTION  (C1).   IB_le_general
WHY THIS FOLLOWS FROM STEP 1. Step 1 identifies the two expressions on the slice; Step 2 shows the slice is the cheapest member of its class.

HOW IT IS CLOSED. Each coordinate contributes at least its magnitude bound squared, by monotonicity of the square on non-negative arguments; summing over S and over its complement and dividing by the positive normaliser gives the claim. No optimiser and no rearrangement argument is needed.
STEP 3 — TIGHTNESS AND NON-BLINDNESS  (C2, C3).   slice_is_tight, Igen_pos_of_ne_zero

WHY THESE FOLLOW FROM STEPS 1–2. Step 1 gives equality on the slice, which is exactly tightness of Step 2's bound. Positivity is immediate from the sum of squares: a single non-zero coordinate suffices, so there is no blind direction.
STEP 4 — THE DESIGN FROM ITS PRICE  (C4).   wB, wPair, budget_exact, weights_unique

HOW IT IS CLOSED. The budget identity is rational algebra valid for every split and every positive price. Uniqueness is the observation that the budget constraint is one linear equation and the split fixes the second, so the pair is determined — there is no free parameter left to fit. Non-negativity of both weights holds exactly on 0 ≤ η ≤ 1 with a positive price, so the admissible range of the split is derived rather than assumed.
STEP 5 — WHERE A TRANSITION CAN OCCUR  (C5).   info_linear, optimum_at_endpoint, transition_at_equal_price
WHY THIS FOLLOWS FROM STEP 4. With the weights determined by (η, c), the delivered information becomes a function of the split alone, and it is affine:

HOW IT IS CLOSED. Substituting the derived weights and collecting terms. An affine function on [0,1] attains its maximum at an endpoint, so the optimal design is pure unless the slope vanishes; the slope vanishes exactly when c·I_B = I_pair, and then every split delivers the same information.
STEP 6 — THE SEPARATION CERTIFICATE ON A CELL.   quadratic_inf_Icc, no_crossing_of_modulus, crossing_bracket

HOW IT IS CLOSED. The continuous x-range is reduced to a three-point check by a quadratic-infimum lemma, and the modulus is propagated across a cell by an exact multiplicative factor. Both verdicts use outward RATIONAL enclosures and exact gaps rather than floating point.
IV.  Results

THE DERIVED WEIGHTS MATCH ALL 24 CELLS EXACTLY. Across q ∈ {8, 16}, μ ∈ {1/4, 2/5}, c ∈ {3/2, 2} and η ∈ {1/3, 13/20, 4/5}, the fitted weights agree with the derived formula in every cell, and the budget identity holds exactly in each. The weights vary with (η, c) and are constant across (q, μ), exactly as the derivation predicts.
THE SEPARATION IS CERTIFIED ON EVERY CELL TESTED. Eight of eight cells certify the strict separation across the whole cell, all of them by the left-endpoint test, with exact rational gaps.

THE PAIR QUERY IS NECESSARY WHEREVER IT IS USED. On 20 parameter cells the A-pair carries positive weight in 17, and in all 17 its necessity is certified: the full value strictly exceeds the best value achievable without it. The three cells without a certificate are exactly those where the pair weight is zero, so nothing is missing — the query is simply not used there.

Fig. 1.  Derived weights against the budget split. Lines are the derived formula; markers are the artifact's own fitted weights in all 24 cells. They coincide exactly, and the weights do not depend on the model parameters.
Fig. 2.  Certificate counts. The three cells without a necessity certificate are exactly those where the pair weight is zero.
V.  Discussion

The two contributions answer objections of different kinds. C1 is a statement about QUANTIFIERS: it converts a slice-quantified lower bound into a class-quantified one, and it is the reason the two-parameter family may now be used without apology. C4 is a statement about PROVENANCE: it replaces a fit with a derivation, so the weights are no longer numbers that happened to work in the cells tested.

C5 is the practical payoff of C4. Once the design is a function of (η, c), the information becomes affine in the split, and an affine objective has no interior optimum — so the design is pure on either side of an explicitly computable threshold. That threshold is where a transition in the design can occur, and it is derived from the model rather than declared.

SCOPE — WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED. The reduction is for the SCALAR query's information; the pair query has a blind direction and is not covered by it. The reduction converts a LOWER bound; an upper bound quantified over the slice would still say nothing about the class. The class is cut out by per-coordinate magnitude constraints, and an alternative set defined otherwise is outside the statement. The information formulas are taken as given and are not re-derived from the sampling model. The derivation is for the uncapped profile; where the unconstrained nuisance minimiser leaves its window the clipped branch applies and is settled separately. No phase boundary is proved.
VI.  Conclusions

The two-parameter alternative family is not a restriction: every alternative in its class costs at least the slice value, and the bound is attained exactly on the slice. The design that reproduces the corpus's coefficients is not fitted: it is forced by the budget constraint and the split, depends only on the split and the price, and makes the delivered information affine — so the optimal design is pure except on an explicitly computable threshold.

Formal corpus behind this poster

The 5 displayed equations are the load-bearing chain, not the corpus. The D6 strand contains 261 Lean source files with 1750 theorem and lemma statements, of which 28 modules carry an acceptance receipt covering 175 declarations whose axiom set was printed and checked. Across the whole programme: 427 files, 3,115 statements, 108 accepted modules, 860 audited declarations.

Every audited declaration was checked to depend only on {propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound}. No module cited by any gate in this work contains a sorry: the seven that exist in the wider repository sit in audit scaffolding and in files named as conjectures, and the overlap with the cited set is empty.

What the poster shows is the shortest path from the problem statement to the claim. The remaining statements are the machinery that path stands on — arithmetic lemmas, measurability side conditions, finite-sum exchanges and the counterexamples that ruled out earlier formulations.
